chunks: From him, from Safwan and Fadalah, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon them both), that he said:
Regarding a man who bought fruit, then sold it before he took possession of it, he said: 'There is no harm (in it).'

key_terms.الثَّمَرَةَ: Fruit (specifically referring to agricultural produce like dates or grapes, often used in fiqh of sales)
key_terms.لاَ بَأْسَ: There is no harm (a common legal phrase indicating permissibility or validity)
key_terms.يَقْبِضَهَا: He takes possession (qabd, a key condition in many types of sales)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to sell fruit before taking possession in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the flexibility in early Islamic commercial law regarding the sale of unharvested fruit (thamar), where physical possession (qabd) is not always a strict prerequisite for validity. It reflects the scholarly consensus that such transactions are permissible provided the fruit is distinct and measurable, illustrating the practical adaptation of fiqh to agricultural commerce in the early Muslim community.
